newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says he feels kinship to Elvis Presley.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says he feels kinship to Elvis Presley.

text.p: President Clinton says he felt a special kinship with that "poor white kid" Elvis Presley because he saw a little bit of himself in the King.

The president talked about his love for all sorts of music and how his job has let him indulge his eclectic interests in a special interview on the VH-1 music video cable channel taped for broadcast Tuesday night.

"I felt a special relationship to Elvis Presley because he was from Mississippi, he was a poor white kid, he sang with a lot of soul. He was sort of my roots," Clinton said, mentioning "Heartbreak Hotel," "Hound Dog," "Don't Be Cruel" and "Love Me Tender" as tunes that struck a chord with him.
Clinton said that during his hardscrabble upbringing in Arkansas, his mother Virginia encouraged him and his half-brother Roger to take up music because "it was something that lifted us up."
"We had some hard times, and we could always get out of them if we had enough good music playing," he said.
Now, Clinton said his job gives him the chance to meet all the entertainers whose music he loves.

"One of the nice things about being president is nearly anybody will come perform for you. So I've gotten to be friends with people that I've loved for 20 or 30 years -- James Taylor, Carly Simon, Barbra Streisand, Aretha Franklin, countless others," he said.
The interview was basically a walk down memory lane for Clinton, the 50-year-old baby boomer who starting playing the clarinet at age 9 and still toots the saxophone.
He said he welcomed the transition of rock and roll from Elvis to the Beatles and was a Rhodes Scholar at Oxford University in Britain when the Beatles broke up.
"Every time I heard 'Let It Be' I remember those endless lines of people who lined up to see the last movie that the Beatles made right when they announced they were breaking up," he said.
Clinton said he is proud of Roger Clinton for continuing to try to make a living as a singer but was glad he did not try to make music a professional career himself.

"I didn't want to have to just do clubs and stay up all night and sleep all day. All the saxophone players I knew did that. Even the ones that made a lot of jazz records basically had their days and nights mixed up, as far as I was concerned," he said.
Plus, he said, "I just wasn't sure I was good enough. I didn't think I would be truly great at it."

It was a certain song and a 1978 visit to the London district of Chelsea that gave Clinton and his wife Hillary the idea for a name for their 17-year-old daughter Chelsea. The song, "Chelsea Morning," was written by Joni Mitchell and sung by Judy Collins.

"One day we were walking in Chelsea and then we started singing that song -- just walking down the street, alone, in Chelsea. And I looked at her and I said, you know, if we have a daughter we ought to name her Chelsea. And that's how we decided to do it," he said.
